claim: Consider two binary classifiers evaluated on data sets with the same total size \(N\) and the same number \(P\) of actual positives. Require every confusion-matrix cell \(TP,FP,FN,TN\) to be strictly positive and require each classifier to be above chance in balanced accuracy, \(B>1/2\). Let \(B=(TP/P+TN/(N-P))/2\) and let \(G=\sqrt{(TP/P)(TN/(N-P))}\) be the sensitivity-specificity G-mean. No pair receives opposite strict rankings from \(B\) and \(G\) for \(N\le10\). Weak-order agreement first fails at \(N=8\), only through a G-mean tie: at \(P=3\), \((1,1,2,4)\) versus \((2,3,1,2)\) has balanced accuracies \(17/30>8/15\) but common \(G^2=4/15\), together with its global class-label complement. At \(N=11\), strict reversal appears for the first time, in exactly six unordered pairs across all prevalences, collapsing under global positive-negative relabeling to three classes. A representative at \(P=3\) is \((1,1,2,7)\) versus \((2,4,1,4)\): balanced accuracy gives \(29/48>7/12\), while \(G^2\) gives \(7/24<1/3\). Writing sensitivity \(s\), specificity \(c\), \(B=(s+c)/2\), and \(\delta=|s-c|/2\), one has \(G^2=B^2-\delta^2\). Thus the strict reversal occurs exactly because the classifier with higher arithmetic-mean class accuracy is sufficiently more imbalanced between the two class accuracies. The all-lower-total claim and the complete first strict layer are exhaustive over all positive-cell fixed-prevalence tables satisfying \(B>1/2\).
integrity: Every admissible integer table through the sharp boundary is enumerated. Balanced accuracy and squared G-mean are compared with exact rational arithmetic. The proof also supplies the structural identity linking arithmetic-mean score, geometric-mean score, and sensitivity-specificity imbalance, plus the determinant characterization of the above-chance domain.
scientific_limitations: The theorem concerns binary confusion matrices with common sample size and prevalence, all four cells strictly positive, and balanced accuracy strictly above one half. It is an exact finite-grid ordering result and does not address statistical uncertainty, tied thresholds, alternative G-mean definitions, or comparisons across prevalences.
title: Eleven cases are the sharp above-chance balanced-accuracy–G-mean strict-reversal boundary
